summary:
This is the **opening page of chapter 14, "Text classification."** The "This chapter covers" box lists three topics:

- An introduction to the field of **natural language processing (NLP)**
- **Preprocessing text input into numeric input**
- **Building simple text classification models**

The introductory paragraph says this chapter lays the foundation for working with text that the *next two chapters* build on (chapter 15, "Language models and the Transformer", and chapter 16, "Text generation"). By the end, you will be able to build a simple text classifier in several different ways, which sets up more complex models such as the Transformer in chapter 15.

Section **14.1, "A brief history of natural language processing,"** then begins. In computer science, human languages such as English or Mandarin are called "natural" to distinguish them from languages designed for machines, such as LISP, Assembly and XML. Every machine language was *designed*: an engineer first wrote down formal rules for which statements are valid and what they mean, and people used the language only once the rules were complete. The sentence "With human language," breaks off at the page end and continues on p.406: *"it's the reverse: usage comes first, and rules arise later."*

**How to use this page:** read it as a roadmap. The chapter outline runs from history (p.405), to text preparation and tokenization (p.408-p.418), to sets versus sequences and the IMDb dataset (p.419-p.421), to set models such as bag-of-words and bigrams (p.422-p.428), and finally to sequence models (RNNs and word embeddings, p.429-p.444).

concepts.name: Natural language processing (NLP)
concepts.definition: Using computers to interpret and manipulate human language (defined on p.406).
concepts.intuition: Teaching machines to work with the messy, evolved languages people actually speak and write.
concepts.technical: Modern NLP is pattern recognition applied to words in text (p.407).
concepts.example: Classifying IMDb reviews as positive or negative.
concepts.misconception: That NLP models understand language the way humans do. The book says they find statistical regularities (p.407).

concepts.name: Text classification
concepts.definition: Predicting a category for an input text.
concepts.intuition: Sorting emails into spam or not spam.
concepts.technical: Requires converting text into numeric tensors first (section 14.2), then training a classifier on them.
concepts.example: Spam detection (p.407), sentiment classification on IMDb (p.420).

questions.question: What three topics does chapter 14 say it covers?
questions.answer: An introduction to NLP, preprocessing text input into numeric input, and building simple text classification models.
questions.explanation: These are the three bullets of the 'This chapter covers' box.

questions.question: According to the page, what distinguishes machine languages like LISP from natural languages?
options: Machine languages were designed: their formal rules came before their use
Natural languages have no rules at all
questions.answer: Machine languages were designed: their formal rules came before their use
questions.explanation: The page says every machine language began with an engineer writing formal rules, and use came after. Vocabulary size isn't mentioned. Machine languages do define meaning. Natural languages do have rules, but they were formalised after the fact (p.406).

questions.question: Why does it matter for NLP that natural language's rules came after its usage?
questions.answer: Because its rules weren't designed upfront, they are incomplete, full of exceptions and constantly changing, so hand-writing a complete rule set is impractical. That motivates learning patterns from data.
questions.explanation: The page sets up this contrast, and p.406 draws the conclusion: natural language is messy, and rule-based systems struggled to generalise.

questions.question: Looking at the chapter outline, can you explain the difference between a 'set model' and a 'sequence model' before reading section 14.3?
questions.answer: Hypothesis to check later: a set model treats a text as an unordered collection of tokens (bag-of-words), while a sequence model processes tokens in order (e.g. an RNN).
questions.explanation: Predicting from the outline primes you for the chapter's central comparison (p.419).

questions.question: Which model does the page say this chapter sets the stage for, and in which chapter does it appear?
questions.answer: The Transformer, in the next chapter (chapter 15, 'Language models and the Transformer').
